PREFACE:
In the scheme of the *Lakṣmīdhara-nibandha*, three sections— [[page 4-to-4]] PREFACE: In the scheme of the *Lakṣmīdhara-nibandha*, three sections—
They occupy key positions, covering in sequence the four *āśramas* or stages of life. In the *Brahmacārīkāṇḍa*,
which is the first section of the *nibandha*, the preparation...
The duties pertaining to the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*) are fully elaborated;
by this, the *saṃskāras* ending with the *samāvartana* are encompassed.
In the *Mokṣakāṇḍa*, which is the final book of the compendium, [the path of liberation is treated].
The path to liberation (*mukti*, *mokṣa*) is addressed in the treatment of the duties of the final two stages of life,
*vānaprastha* and *saṃnyāsa*. Entering these two final stages.
It is not mandatory even for the "twice-born" (dvija). It is closed to women as well as Śūdras; however, liberation (mukti) is open to everyone, regardless of āśrama, caste (varṇa), or gender.
One who strictly observes the duties and way of life prescribed for the householder may attain liberation (*mokṣa*) without entering the final stage (*saṃnyāsāśrama*). In the first, third...

And in the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*), one is no longer of the world but stands outside it. Since marriage is the preparation for the stage of the householder (*gārhasthya*), both sexes are envisioned therein.
The fulfillment of the duties of the second āśrama is also the only āśrama accessible to every varṇa; it encompasses the greatest and most important portion of an individual’s life.
Without it, the stability and continued existence of human society would be impossible. Whereas, in the Hindu theory of society, social equilibrium is held to result from...

The maintenance of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) is no less a fundamental tenet of the Hindu social creed than the principle that all duties— indeed, all things— are [ultimately one].
The final refuge is established upon that of the householder (*gṛhastha*);
his religious and ritual duties are aimed at maintaining contact with the "past" and...
‘the future,’ with divine or superhuman beings and with V1 [page 5–to–5]
[He should offer] to subhuman beings, to all members of society, and to all living beings; [he should perform] the Agnihotra, the Śrāddha, the twenty-one sacrifices,
and the Vaiśvadeva (in which the householder is engaged).
Joined to provide food even for dogs and *caṇḍālas*,
reflecting the duty of universal benevolence and compassion,
[it includes] the installation and worship of deities and the Supreme [Being].

For those who are excluded from [the practice of] consecration (*pratisthā*) and worship (*pūjā*), the utilization of charity and gifts (*dāna*), pilgrimages (*tīrthayātrā*), and religious observances (*vrata*), [this is prescribed].

forming rites and sacrifices according to gender, social status, or economic condition as means of grace, and performing pacificatory (*śānti*) and penitential rites that secure the required [results].

The standards of purity (*śuddhi*, *prāyaścitta*) are all rooted in the householder stage (*gārhasthya*). The student, the forest-dweller, and the ascetic lie outside the scope of civil rights and political obligations.
The householder is the only effective member of the state, and the only person who will normally require the protection of the courts of law to enforce his legal rights.

He alone will normally fall within the scope of *vyavahāra* and *rājanīti*. Thus, the section on *gārhasthya* (the householder's life) constitutes the logical prelude to all other sections dealing with these subjects.
The ordinary and occasional or special duties of the common citizen constitute the keystone in the arch of *dharma*. Among the authors of the *nibandhas*, Lakṣmīdhara alone...
With the sole exception of Caṇḍeśvara, who merely copies him,
[the author] has recognized the foundational status of the householder’s dharma within the Hindu scheme of existence— that is, of life— and...
of the hereafter; others have followed a haphazard sequence. In the Indian view, the true significance and meaning of wealth and well-being, as well as of the ultimate—
Reality may arise either from intuition or through the discipline of a regulated life in the world. Those who hold the former view consider the gifted student to be...
A *brahmacārin* may proceed directly to the life of an anchorite (*vānaprastha*) by virtue of possessing this intuitive knowledge (*jñāna*); however,
most authorities maintain that only one who has completed the student stage [is so entitled].
V11 He who proceeds from one stage of life to another (āśramād āśramam).
One may attain true understanding by virtue of the discipline and knowledge arising from each stage of experience;
as a statesman, Lakṣmīdhara is unable to perceive [this].
With equanimity, he avoids the racial suicide involved in the spread of universal asceticism or cenobitism; he therefore rejects the view in favor of immediate entry into *saṃnyāsa*.
After the period of studentship, he insists upon the necessity of fully experiencing the discipline of family life for the sake of grasping reality and attaining liberation.
In the Hindu scheme, family life is not intended to be one of unalloyed pleasure and sense gratification; rather,
life is a dedication, and every stage of it marks an important milestone.

Regarding the aspects of dedication: it is only within the family that a person can attain their full development; for without the fulfillment of social and spiritual duties, the mere practice of austerity is insufficient.
Obligations alone cannot lead to liberation; a virtue born within the shelter of rigid asceticism is no true virtue,
for it has not been tested and tempered in the fire of experience.

When weighed in the balance, the householder’s life (*gārhasthya*) outweighs all other modes of life; as in Manu’s polemical arguments against the *śūdra*’s renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), [it is shown that] the life of the householder is superior.

One may observe an animosity toward the Buddhist rule that opened *saṃnyāsa* to all— both men and women, as well as both *vipras* and non-*vipras*— which threatened the very foundation of the community and its primary economic support.
Thus, in Lakṣmīdhara’s marshaling of the authorities extolling the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama), we may perceive the statesman enforcing the means for the stabilization of society.
The householder stage (gārhasthya) makes marriage a sacramental obligation for women and a social duty for men.
Neither a widower, nor a bachelor, nor an anchorite can perform important rites; a plurality of wives is not required when one wife fulfills the needs of ritualistic practice.
As a rule of ordinary life, monogamy follows as a duty;
for a woman, marriage is a *saṃskāra*, and the approach to matrimony requires regulation that is detailed and minute.
As on pages 7 through 7,
The bride’s virginity is the complement to the groom’s premarital chastity; the selection of lifelong partners must be made after careful consideration of eugenics and other relevant factors.
Since the social purpose of marriage is progeny, whatever shall frustrate that end must invalidate the union;
therefore, tests of potency are indicated for application.
The rules of endogamy and exogamy, the significance of some of which is no longer apparent— such as the absolute prohibition against the union of *sagotra* lineages— are detailed.
Lakṣmīdhara is opposed to *sapinda* unions and would reject cross-cousin marriages, for which ancient custom is cited as an authority in certain regions; he likewise opposes inter-caste unions.

The conditions that invalidate marriages— which are generally treated in the section on civil law (*vyavahāra*)— are here negated within the detailed discussion of the householder’s stage of life (*gārhasthya*).
This demonstrates the importance Lakṣmīdhara attaches to a proper union for both ritual and civil purposes;
the rites of marriage are described with meticulous precision.
The rule of pre-puberty marriage is relaxed to the extent of declaring— as Shakespeare did— that "the wife must be younger. This reflects both the piety of a priest and the precision of a judge.
The critical recitation of the characteristics of the traditional forms of marriage is clearly intended to condemn their degradation through purely animalistic motives.
And even by instinctual impulses as well as mercenary considerations;
for a contract degrades marriage just as fraud, force, or sale do, though it does not annul it. This is the consideration regarding women.
This is a characteristic of Dharma; it is reflected in the rules protecting the bride in cases where her interests might otherwise be sacrificed, as well as in the imposition of an interval.
Between the wedding and its consummation,
and in the rare and specified cases where a second wife was permitted, as well as by the principle of *parivedana*, which penalizes those who...

To cause the marriage of a younger sister (or brother) to precede that of the elder; for the wife is the essential partner. "Let a woman still marry one who is older than herself" (Twelfth Night II, iv, 29–30).
She may officiate at domestic and occasional rites.
Her husband is absent, yet a husband cannot function at all in any religious rite without his wife.
This illustrates the intimate connection between the powers of the seen and...
The existence of unseen forces and their cooperation for mutual well-being is a tenet of Hindu faith; the performance of the numerous daily rites of the householder secures benefits that—
It is not only for him, but for the community as a whole;
the distribution of benefits imposes a reciprocal responsibility upon the partners. For one whose means are insufficient for...

Through the proper performance of prescribed ritual duties, one may seek the necessary assistance from the wealthy (yet virtuous) members of the community and from its leader. [In the event of] a lack of means...
Under such circumstances, this cannot serve as an excuse for the neglect of one's duty; rather,
the responsibility rests upon the householder of the first varṇa, even though members of the other two varṇas are present.
There is also a similar obligation: "A life of leisure or ease does not belong to a conscientious householder, even if he were a universal monarch (cakravartin);
rather, it diminishes one's independence in the constancy of practice."
The state of being a householder for those who maintain the sacred fires is fraught with obstacles such as the burden of maintaining carts.
1. In modern life, occupation determines one’s duties;
in the Hindu Dharma, it is the reverse.
It determines occupation. In any scheme of social planning, a loss of the freedom to act as one pleases is implicit.
*Varnāśramadharma* is social planning based upon the eternal.
The duties of the Brāhmaṇa determine the occupations open to him in normal times. The six...
The chapters dealing with the duties and occupations of the *vipra* bring to light the incorrectness of the now prevalent view of [the brahmin] as a privileged and comfortable class.
The nature of his position at the head of society as teacher,
priest in sacrifices, and donee is both obligatory and honorary. [Regarding] promiscuous mendicancy and the solicitation...
Even the acceptance of gifts freely is prohibited.
(Uttararāmacarita, Act I, Śl. 8b)
His daily rites, the benefits of which the community receives,
One should not provide him with any remuneration;
he is enjoined to lead a life of graduated poverty or austerity,
as economic occupations that yield income or profit are closed to him.
He cannot be a king; he cannot accept assistance beyond what is absolutely necessary, for the other *varṇas* [are responsible] for the duties of protection and the acquisition of wealth.
While assigned duties are more rigid and ascetic, open occupations are less so.
Beyond these specific duties, every human being,
both as an individual and as a member of society, possesses general duties.
Of a moral kind, they may consist in observances (*niyama*) or restraints (*yama*). The enumeration and discussion of these in several chapters lay them bare.
The ethical code by which every Hindu is bound does not allow for any deviation. The constituent elements of a moral life are subjected to rigorous analysis and are articulated with clarity.
Lakṣmī rejects with caustic rigor all casuistry involving the assumption of conflicts between duties or permissible deviations from the path of rectitude, as well as emptiness and fulness.

Dhara’s exposition of the moral obligations of the common householder (*gṛhastha*) displays the high level of Hindu ethics; by adhering to such a rigorous moral code, the first *varṇa* [fulfills its duty].
It is to set an example; thus, its austerity, poverty,
and moral rectitude earn for it an exaltation of status as compensation for the loss of material benefits.

And a life of comfort and self-regarding ease; conversely, he who acts contrary to the social code forfeits his entitlement to his own *varṇa* or to any *varṇa* whatsoever, and becomes an outcast (*patita*).
Social pressure is exerted upon the *patita* (the outcaste) not out of malice, but in order to reclaim him through repentance,
expiation, and rehabilitation for the sake of maintaining ethical integrity.
Or social standards— even those who defy or violate the moral code, including one's closest relatives, must be abandoned.
The interests of the community, especially its spiritual and...
Moral interests are paramount; they take precedence over the inclinations or wishes of the individual.
Thus conceived and lived, family life (*gārhasthya*) becomes a dedication to the highest ends of existence.
Its end is not vulgar pleasure, but happiness of a real and lasting character; dharma has no use for hedonism. The attainment of the knowledge of reality is the highest end.
Regarding human effort: if one leads a life not of the passive,
contemplative quietist or recluse, but of an active worker, acting within and for society while discharging one's duties with devotion (*śraddhā*).

Having performed the prescribed acts of piety and discharged the debt to the ancestors from whom he derives his material being, he enters [the world] to fulfill his obligations to the lineage by assisting in its continuation.
The wedded estate, acknowledging through prayer and worship his devotion to the Supreme, and through the cultivation and dissemination of knowledge, discharging his obligations on their behalf.
He would fulfill the duties of a true householder (*gṛhastha*) toward the seers (*ṛṣi*), from whom the culture of the lineage has sprung, by means of the preservation of his lineage.

The cultivation of culture, moral standards, and spirituality constitutes the primary duty of the householder. It is this very recognition of the exalted destiny of family life within the Hindu framework of *dharma* that provides [the foundation].
This distinction, made in Lakṣmīdhara’s *Gṛhasthakāṇḍa*,
vindicates his wisdom in establishing it as a separate and major section of his great digest, as well as its foundational importance.
This act reflects the burning conviction of the Royal Guru and the wisdom of the preeminent statesman of his kingdom and era.
It remains for me to recount with gratitude my obligations in the preparation of an edition of a work that has been virtually lost; for the editor, the first duty is the collection [of manuscripts].
In order to secure an authentic text from among all surviving manuscripts,
the difficulty of overcoming such fundamental [obstacles]—
A mental obstacle can be realized only by those who have had to surmount it. That I have been able to do so is due to the generous help I have received from my obligations.
In this regard, my deepest gratitude is owed to Sir V. T. Krishnamacharya, K.C.I.E., who employed his great influence to secure for me copies of the manuscripts from Udaipur and Bikanir.

Hārīta says that for the purpose of delivering one from the gods, through the refinement [of initiation], one attains equality with the gods.

He attains the same world and union [with them]. Therefore, they say that one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is indeed equal to a god. Day after day he gratifies [the gods], for they purify him day after day, morning and evening.

Day after day, with Agni as their mouth, they wait upon him morning and evening with oblations. Therefore, even among those who know the sacrificial offerings (havirvid), one who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) becomes most meritorious, even if others have not.

He goes; therefore, they say that this fire is equal to the gods. He enters into the worlds of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* verses, and into the luminaries, or he is established in Brahman; for he causes this [fire] to reach them every day, evening and morning.

A sacrifice performed by those of mixed character is inevitably flawed; it leaks away, and the sacrificer encounters misfortunes and enters all wombs, or his life-span is cut short. "They complete his sacrifice, which yields all desires, with sacrificial fees"—thus he gives the sacrificial fee; by that, he sacrifices to the world of the moon. As for what [is given] to the Hotṛ... the fire—

By that which he gives to the Udgātṛ, he wins the world of Parjanya; by that which he gives to the Hotṛ and the reciters (praśastṛ), he wins the quarters of space; by that which he gives to those who perform favors (anugrahakartṛ), he wins this world;
by that which he gives to the obedient and learned (anūcāna) student, he wins the heavenly world; and by as much land as he gives, he wins the removal of afflictions.

The moon is indeed the Brahman; as long as the moon does not wane, so long is his sacrifice [effective].

One should not sell pippalī, marīca, grain, meat, weapons, or the hope for merit; specifically, one should not sell sesame or rice among grains.

Regarding this, Manu says:
"There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, conquest, investment, performance of work, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous."

‘Means of acquiring wealth’ (vittāgamāḥ) refers to methods for obtaining riches. ‘Inheritance’ (dāyaḥ) is wealth acquired through lineage. ‘Gain’ (lābhaḥ) refers to [finding] buried treasure and the like. ‘Victory’ (jayaḥ) here means the overcoming of an enemy in battle. ‘Lending’ (prayogaḥ) refers to usury. ‘Application of labor’ (karmayogaḥ) refers to agriculture, trade, and so forth.

Ownership arises through inheritance, purchase, partition, seizure, or discovery; among these, what is obtained by a Brāhmaṇa is termed "acquired" (labdha); for a Kṣatriya, it is "conquered" (vijita);
and for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is "earned" (nirviṣṭa).

"Partition" (*saṃvibhāga*) refers to the inheritance from a friend; this is the view of Bhartṛyajña. "Acquisition" (*parigraha*) refers to wild buffaloes and the like that have not previously belonged to another. "Discovery" (*adhigama*) refers to what is obtained from mines and similar sources.

[30 392] [[page 543-to-543]] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the eye as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive forms as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive eye-contact as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive feeling born of eye-contact as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the earth element as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive ignorance as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive generosity as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the fruit of a Stream-enterer as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the state of a Buddha as having an intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, become one who has set out for full enlightenment? How does he train in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive the perfection of giving as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as having an intrinsic nature, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or great compassion as having an intrinsic nature. He does not perceive the knowledge of all modes as having an intrinsic nature. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One replied: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, if all dharmas were not empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva would not be able to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. But because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, training in all dharmas as being empty of intrinsic nature, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. likewise, according to the Śatapatha Śruti.
"The world says that a son is one who has been instructed; therefore, they say one should instruct him.
In the Āditya Purāṇa it is said:
"Having seen the face of your grandson, why do you grieve?"
For one who is immersed in the great cycle of existence, there is indeed no fear other than that of hell.
Having discharged his debts to the great sages, the ancestors, and the gods in due order,
and having entrusted everything to his son, he may dwell maintaining an attitude of neutrality.
Alone, one should constantly contemplate what is beneficial for oneself in solitude;
contemplating alone, O Brahmin, one attains the supreme good.

"Equanimity" (*mādhyasthya*) means the relinquishing of the sense of "mine" regarding wealth, children, and so forth. "Solitary" (*ekākī*) means without companions, such as fellow students and the like. "Avoiding conversation and the like," he should contemplate his own welfare; the meaning is that he should meditate upon the nature of Brahman as described in the Upaniṣads.
The gods know him as an elder who has abandoned and relinquished his home and residence, who is liberated from former kinsmen, who has conquered his senses, and who is free from greed.
For it is while reflecting thus— this being the reading in the *Kullūka-bhāṣya* [page 586–586]— that one acts.
In the section on the householder’s life,
260] states: This eternal mode of conduct for a Brahmin householder has been declared.
And the ritual rules for the Snātaka vows, which increase one's inner strength and are auspicious.
A Brahmin who lives according to this conduct, being learned in the Vedas and the Shastras,
is eternally freed from sin and is glorified in the world of Brahma.
[5.169] By this rule, he should never neglect the five sacrifices;
a Brāhmaṇa should dwell in his home during the second stage of his life.
[4-1] Having lived the first quarter of his life with his teacher,
the twice-born man should enter into marriage and dwell in the household during the second quarter of his life.

435. Thus, upon considering such statements, it follows that for a householder alone who has discharged the three debts, who is capable of maintaining his family and so forth, and whose son [is likewise capable], there is the retinue consisting of wife and others.
For one who has become capable of abandoning the sense of "mine" and has performed the superimposition [of identity] upon the Self— being thus constituted,

either by being devoid of a wife or by having ceased the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and having desisted from rites such as the *śrāddha* which require material substances, [he remains devoted to] the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), the water-libation (*udakatarpaṇa*), and purification (*śauca*).
Medhātithi maintains that this method applies to one who performs the practice through mere mental reflection.

Thus ends the section on the Householder (*gṛhasthakāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Lakṣmīdhara, son of Bhaṭṭa Śrī Hṛdayadhara, the Great Minister for Peace and War under the illustrious Mahārāja Śrīmad Govindacandradeva.
